macro: News flow this week favored the bears as yields surged and Brent crude rose above $100, though the S&P 500 and Nasdaq pushed higher on AI enthusiasm surrounding Meta's personal AI agent Muse. The single biggest macro event was the September flash PMIs, which came in scorching hot — pointing to healthy growth but triggering a 15 basis point surge in 10-year yields on Wednesday, along with higher inflation, margin headwinds, and supply chain conditions among the most stressed in decades outside of peak COVID. The Trump-Xi meeting was largely a nonevent, extending the existing US-China trade truce by two months with nothing additional to show for it.
rates_fed: Ten-year yields surged 15 basis points on Wednesday alone following the hot September flash PMI release, with secular upward pressure on yields driven by resilient growth, elevated inflation, AI-related debt issuance, and extreme fiscal imbalances. Central banks globally continue to tighten, with Norway hiking 25 basis points Thursday and markets pricing greater than 50% odds of rate hikes from the Bank of Canada on October 28th, the FOMC on October 28th, the ECB on October 29th, and the Bank of England on November 5th. Fed officials have been issuing daily warnings about upside inflation risks and the need for further policy tightening.
market_outlook: Adam's lean is cautiously bearish — stocks are holding in largely due to TACO dynamics and Muse-driven AI enthusiasm, but the underlying macro backdrop is deteriorating with yields spiking, oil above $100, unresolved geopolitical conflicts, and mounting headwinds to the data center boom that underpins much of the current earnings cycle. The key catalyst to watch is whether the US-Iran diplomatic process produces a tangible breakthrough that brings oil prices lower, which would be the single most powerful relief valve for the market.
bull_case: The bull argument centers on the idea that all macro problems trace back to oil, and Trump — being transactional and non-ideological — could reverse the situation at any moment by returning to the terms of the June MOU. The underlying US economy is holding up remarkably well, as confirmed by the strong September flash PMIs, supported by an AI boom that just received a major boost from Meta's Muse and the mainstream adoption of personal AI agents. Management teams at sell-side conferences throughout September have struck a constructive tone, setting up what could be a solid Q3 earnings season. Additionally, US-Iran negotiations at the UN General Assembly were the most substantive in weeks, raising hopes for a near-term deal.
bear_case: Equities appear to be whistling past the graveyard, ignoring surging oil prices above $100 and spiking borrowing costs that pose real threats to corporate margins and the debt-funded data center boom. The Iran conflict shows no sign of a final resolution — Trump lacks the will to kinetically escalate, Iran is increasingly stubborn and divided, and the Houthis have opened a dangerous new front in Yemen, while the Ukraine-Russia war continues to disrupt global energy supply. The secular forces pushing yields higher — resilient growth, hot inflation, AI-driven debt supply, and fiscal imbalances — are not going away anytime soon. Muse-driven AI optimism is masking a string of negative industry developments including delayed IPOs, massive cash burn, frontier competition, data center moratoriums, construction delays, and Oracle's force majeure declaration.

company_items.summary: Meta's personal AI agent Muse dominated the week's AI narrative, breaking personal AI agents into the mainstream consumer market and creating a new source of compute demand that propelled AI-linked stocks higher. However, Adam flags that Muse enthusiasm may not be sustainable as a flood of competing personal AI agents is likely coming in the weeks ahead, potentially as soon as OpenAI's Dev Day on September 29th. The optimism is also masking broader negative industry developments including delayed IPOs, reports of huge cash burn, and fierce frontier competition.

McDonald's shares were hit hard following this week's analyst meeting after management warned that comparable sales are pacing slightly below expectations in Q3. The company also announced plans to significantly increase capital spending, which will meaningfully reduce free cash flow conversion — a double negative for the stock.

AutoZone reported comparable sales that fell short of expectations, representing an underwhelming earnings result that weighed on the stock. The miss added to a pattern of consumer-facing companies struggling to meet elevated Street estimates.

Darden reported comparable sales misses at both its Olive Garden and LongHorn Steakhouse concepts, disappointing investors who had expected more resilient consumer spending at casual dining. The shortfall across multiple brands signals broader softness in the casual dining segment.

KB Home issued weak fiscal Q4 guidance amid continued headwinds in the housing market, raising concerns about the near-term trajectory of homebuilder earnings. The guidance cut reflects the combined pressure of elevated mortgage rates and affordability constraints weighing on new home demand.

Paychex disappointed with its Management Solutions business posting revenue below Wall Street expectations, an underwhelming result for what is typically viewed as a steady, predictable compounder. The miss raises questions about whether small business hiring and payroll activity is beginning to soften.

TD SYNNEX shares were hit following its earnings release, with weak gross margins the primary culprit for investor disappointment. The margin miss highlights the input cost and pricing pressure dynamic flagged broadly in the September flash PMIs.

Oracle declared force majeure on data center commitments, cited as one of several negative recent developments in the AI infrastructure build-out that Muse enthusiasm has overshadowed. This is a meaningful signal of stress in the data center supply chain that could have read-across implications for hyperscalers and their suppliers.

sectors: AI and data center infrastructure stocks were lifted by Meta Muse enthusiasm, but Adam warns the sector faces mounting headwinds including delayed IPOs, massive cash burn, fierce frontier model competition, data center moratoriums and construction delays, and Oracle's force majeure — all at a time when the US economy has never been more levered to a single industry. Housing remains under pressure as evidenced by KB Home's weak guidance. Casual dining showed cracks with Darden's comp misses across multiple brands. Global central bank tightening continues to tighten financial conditions broadly, with rate hike odds rising for the Fed, ECB, Bank of Canada, and Bank of England over the next five weeks.

tts_summary:
Here's the weekly recap for the week ended Friday September 25th, 2026.

Bottom line on the bull versus bear debate this week: the bears had the better of the argument on the news flow, even though stocks didn't fully cooperate. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq pushed higher, but it was almost entirely driven by artificial intelligence enthusiasm around Meta's new personal agent called Muse — not by any genuine macro improvement. Underneath the surface, yields surged, Brent crude stayed above one hundred dollars a barrel, and supply chain conditions hit levels of stress not seen since peak COVID.

The single biggest macro event of the week was the September flash purchasing managers index data, which came in scorching hot. Strong growth readings, yes — but the bond market immediately repriced, with ten-year yields jumping fifteen basis points in a single session on Wednesday. Add in hotter inflation readings, corporate margin pressure from input costs rising faster than selling prices, and extreme supply chain disruptions, and this was not a clean bullish print.

On rates and the Fed, the global tightening cycle is accelerating. Norway hiked twenty-five basis points Thursday. Markets are now pricing greater than fifty percent odds of rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England over the next five weeks. Fed officials have been warning daily about upside inflation risks and the need for more tightening. The secular forces pushing yields higher — resilient growth, hot inflation, artificial intelligence debt issuance flooding markets, and massive fiscal imbalances — show no signs of reversing.

Now to the key company stories. Meta's Muse was the dominant narrative, breaking personal AI agents into the mainstream consumer market and driving a wave of enthusiasm across artificial intelligence linked equities. But Adam is skeptical this optimism is sustainable — a flood of competing agents is likely coming fast, potentially as soon as OpenAI's developer day on September 29th. Meanwhile, the broader artificial intelligence infrastructure picture quietly deteriorated this week: delayed initial public offerings, reports of huge cash burn, fierce frontier model competition, additional data center moratoriums, construction delays, and Oracle declaring force majeure on data center commitments. That last one is significant and deserves more attention than it's getting.

On the earnings front, it was a rough week for company-specific results. McDonald's got hit hard after management warned comparable sales are running below expectations in the third quarter and announced a major step-up in capital spending that will compress free cash flow. AutoZone, Darden — with misses at both Olive Garden and LongHorn — KB Home on weak forward guidance, Paychex on a Management Solutions revenue miss, and TD SYNNEX on weak gross margins all disappointed.

Geopolitically, US-Iran diplomacy saw its most substantive engagement in weeks at the United Nations General Assembly, with Tehran reportedly proposing a return to the June memorandum of understanding within seven days. The bull case says Trump, being purely transactional, could flip the oil situation overnight by accepting that kind of deal. The bear case says the stalemate will persist, the Houthis have opened a dangerous new front in Yemen, and the Russia-Ukraine war continues to hammer global refined product supply.

Directional outlook: lean cautiously bearish. Stocks are being held up by artificial intelligence mania and the hope that Trump engineers a quick oil fix — neither of which is a durable foundation. Watch the Iran diplomacy track and any signals from the Federal Reserve as the primary catalysts for the week ahead.
